extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, safety and compliance officers, trade associations, and commenters on OSHA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and supporting analyses for revising OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) to align with GHS Rev. 7, including legal authority, risk and feasibility determinations, economic and industry impact analyses, and specific regulatory changes (classification, labeling, SDSs, training).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best available evidence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must use the “best available evidence,” which includes “the latest available scientific data in the field”; “research, demonstrations, experiments, and such other information as may be appropriate”; and “experience gained under this and other health and safety laws.” (29 U.S.C. 655(f); 29 U.S.C. 655(b)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the most current scientific data, research, demonstrations, experiments, and relevant experience when supporting a standards decision; standards must be based on the record as a whole and the best available evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(b)(5) standard-setting mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(b)(5) requires that in promulgating health standards dealing with toxic materials or harmful physical agents, the Secretary must “set the standard which most adequately assures, to the extent feasible, on the basis of the best available evidence, that no employee will suffer material impairment of health or functional capacity even if such employee has regular exposure . . . for the period of his working life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once OSHA determines a significant risk is present and can be reduced by a standard, section 6(b)(5) requires issuance of the standard that ‘most adequately assures’ protection subject only to feasibility considerations; worker health is prioritized over other considerations except where attainment is unachievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(b)(7) labeling and warning authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(b)(7) provides that standards shall prescribe the use of labels or other appropriate forms of warning as are necessary to insure that employees are apprised of all hazards to which they are exposed, relevant symptoms and appropriate emergency treatment, and proper conditions and precautions of safe use or exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling and employee warnings are basic protections—especially when no specific permissible exposure limits exist—and the statute's last sentence permits modifications to labeling/warning requirements via rulemaking where warranted by experience, information, or medical/technological developments acquired since promulgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 8 recordkeeping and rulemaking authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 8(c)(1) empowers the Secretary to require employers to make, keep, and preserve records regarding activities related to the OSH Act; section 8(g)(2) empowers the Secretary to 'prescribe such rules and regulations as he may deem necessary to carry out [his] responsibilities' under the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA may rely on these provisions to require recordkeeping and to issue necessary regulatory text supporting the HCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant risk determination and nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA previously determined that the HCS substantially reduces a significant risk of material harm (inadequate communication is itself a hazard). Where a general significant-risk finding supports a standard, OSHA need not make a new significant-risk finding for every provision; a requirement must be reasonably related to the purpose of the standard as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule provisions should be shown to be reasonably related to the HCS's purpose; cite precedent (e.g., Benzene, Lead I, Cotton Dust) to justify reliance on earlier significant-risk findings rather than fresh per-provision findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility requirement (to the extent feasible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because section 6(b)(5) imposes the 'to the extent feasible' limitation, feasibility analyses are required. Feasibility has two aspects: technological feasibility (protective measures exist or can reasonably be developed) and economic feasibility (industry can absorb or pass on costs without threatening long-term profitability or competitive structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate both technological and economic feasibility in the record; discuss feasibility analyses in the preamble (see referenced sections VI.E and VI.G). OSHA may not rely on cost-benefit balancing to set the standard, but must assess economic feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Orders and OIRA review compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: E.O. 12866 (as amended) defines 'significant regulatory action' and triggers OMB/OIRA review; E.O. 13563 directs agencies to adopt regulations only upon a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs and to tailor regulations to impose the least burden consistent with objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though OSHA cannot use cost-benefit analysis to set standards under 6(b)(5), the agency still estimates costs and benefits to comply with E.O. 12866/13563 and to determine whether a rule is a 'significant regulatory action.' Include quantitative estimates (where possible) and qualitative discussion of non-quantifiable values (equity, fairness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for regulation / necessity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS is necessary because employees are exposed to chemical hazards that can cause serious injury, illness, and death. The HCS ensures employers and employees have information they need through mandatory hazard classification, labeling, SDSs, and label updating requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the continuing presence of hazards and the inadequacy of voluntary market forces to ensure timely alignment with an updated GHS; show that regulatory action improves worker protection and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain alignment with GHS Rev. 7
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisions maintain alignment with the GHS by adding classification categories (aerosols, desensitized explosives, flammable gases) and updating select hazard and precautionary statements to provide clearer and more precise hazard information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how alignment promotes international trade, standardization, and improved hazard communication; explain why regulation (not voluntary market action) is necessary to maintain uniformity as GHS is periodically revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address implementation issues identified with 2012 HCS
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisions address practical issues identified in implementing the 2012 HCS, including updating labeling requirements for small containers, packaged containers released for shipment or constituting bulk shipping, and allowing withholding of concentration ranges for trade-secret reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how specific updates resolve prior implementation problems and consider the compliance burden and benefits of each targeted change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic impact accounting categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The FEA categorizes costs and cost savings into five main categories: (1) cost of reclassifying chemicals and revising SDSs and labels to conform with Appendix changes; (2) management familiarization and related costs; (3) employee training costs necessitated by changes (paragraph (h)(1) of 2012 HCS); (4) cost savings from the released-for-shipment provision (paragraph (f)(11)); and (5) cost savings from limiting labeling for certain very small containers (proposed paragraph (f)(12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the first three as one-time costs and the latter two as recurring annual savings; provide quantification (annualized net cost savings at specified discount rates) and explain assumptions used in cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and affected-entity profiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify affected NAICS industries, number of affected entities and establishments, number of 'affected relevant employees,' and average revenues/profits for affected entities and establishments; provide separate estimates for small entities (per SBA) and 'very small' entities (OSHA: <20 employees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BLS and U.S. Census data to populate tables (VI-1 through VI-3), explain methodology and data sources, and discuss implications for small and very small entities (regulatory flexibility analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for estimating SDSs and labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate SDSs per establishment (from prior analyses/sampling), multiply by establishments and firms to get total SDSs; for labels, start with shipment weight by commodity class, estimate average weight per container, allocate tons to container sizes, divide by average container weight to get number of containers, multiply by average labels per container to estimate total labels, and allocate labels to NAICS codes using receipts data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document data sources (CFS, Census, BLS), list steps clearly, disclose where professional judgment is used (e.g., typical product weight/container weight) and update baseline data (e.g., 2017 CFS) as available; explain limitations and rounding approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very small container labeling exception conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under proposed paragraph (f)(12)(iii), only a product identifier is required on very small containers (3 ml or less) where the manufacturer, importer, or distributor can demonstrate that a label would interfere with normal use and that it is not feasible to use pull-out labels, fold-back labels, or tags containing the full label information; the immediate outer packaging must include the full label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify burden of proof for demonstrating infeasibility and ensure the outer packaging contains full label information; quantify affected labels and containers when estimating cost savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Released-for-shipment labeling provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisions include a 'released-for-shipment' provision (paragraph (f)(11)) that affects labeling requirements for packaged containers released for shipment, producing cost savings for manufacturers, importers, and distributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'released for shipment' and calculate cost savings separately for shipments from manufacturers and distributors; explain allocation method in label accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements and estimations
rubrics_metrics.description: Training is required as necessitated by changes to the HCS (referencing paragraph (h)(1) of the 2012 HCS). OSHA estimates training costs for health and safety personnel and assumes only trivial additional training for most users of reclassified chemicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SOC occupations (e.g., production occupations, logisticians) and BLS employment data to estimate numbers requiring new training; document assumptions about who needs training and why training for users may be minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional judgment and transparency about assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where data are lacking (e.g., percentage of products shipped by container type), OSHA and its contractor used professional judgment to select 'typical' product weight per gallon and container weight; commenters did not provide contradictory data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose where judgment is used, explain rationale, and invite/publicly consider commenter input; record changes to rounding and significant-digit reporting that affect estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity and trade-facilitation rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The GHS is a 'uniformity standard' for presenting hazard information; maintaining uniform hazard information with the GHS improves efficiency, effectiveness, and international trade and helps emergency responders and workers who lack a market relationship with manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that market forces alone will not ensure timely alignment with periodic GHS revisions and that regulation is needed to avoid long transition periods and protect workers and responders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of construction and downstream users
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the PEA did not include construction (NAICS 23) within scope, OSHA notes construction is not exempt and potential construction impacts are likely downstream consumption effects; OSHA evaluates whether training costs for downstream users are de minimis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stakeholders (e.g., Construction Industry Safety Coalition) raise scope concerns, explain the basis for inclusion/exclusion and quantify downstream impacts where feasible.
